The Consequences of Poor Design: 
A Critique of the Systems 
Experiment 
Harlow — July 20, 2026, edited by: retrooper & Mila
IMSC: S-HW-2
Preface 
While I was writing this essay, Turtle approached me and asked me to take over the 
operation of the Systems Experiment. I accepted, as I want to see the IMS and this event 
succeed. This is, of course, a potential conflict of interest, but I chose to disclose this 
information here because it is relevant to the context of this critique. For this reason, I also 
ask that you scrutinize this essay under that context. Though, I will not alter the language or 
any of my critiques in the essay to accommodate this change. Will I implement any 
significant measures in the event to offset the problems I bring up? Probably not. I’ll try to 
communicate more to the best of my ability, but at this point in the event, it would be actively 
counterproductive and would also go against what I argue for. However, I welcome and will 
encourage people to criticize how I then run it. 
Minecraft Server Theory arguably began with someone who actually put their theory 
into practice. PineconeLP’s “Raid Farms” has been discussed at length in the IMS, whether in 
passing or as the focus of an entire essay or video—there’s no doubt that it's influential. 
However, having only one example of a server using MST in its design becomes quite 
problematic in the long term for the field. As a result of this, there’s a large amount of people 
in the IMS who’ve expressed wanting to experiment more, thereby putting more ideas into 
practice. This is difficult, of course, because running a server takes a lot of time and money, 
time and money that people don’t have. And that’s not even taking into account whether or 
not people want to run control studies or get studies peer-reviewed. For this reason, there

Harlow 2
have not been many experiments. 
The Systems Experiment is an event run by Turtle (turtle2770), an administrator at the 
IMS, who set out to create a space to run experiments. Unfortunately, the event fails at this 
goal. What could’ve been an environment, where members of the IMS could test their 
systems, was not. This essay is a look into what exactly went wrong and an urge to do right 
in the future. In writing this critique, I acknowledge that Turtle has a lot on his plate at the 
moment, and I sympathize with him as someone who often plans events myself. This is not a 
criticism directed at Turtle or any of the other organizers of the event; I have immense 
respect for their efforts. The Systems Experiment is an example of a well-intentioned, 
however, very flawed attempt at experimental research—flaws caused by its lack of adequate 
communication, ad hoc decision making, and lack of scientific integrity. 
Effective communication is the foundation of any good event, and really any sort of 
social activity. Communication can make or break the success of an event. And it’s 
unfortunately one of the biggest flaws of the Systems Experiment. Outlining well-defined 
goals is a prerequisite for effective communication. While the goals of the event were 
described in the Manual and Handbook, most people seemingly hadn’t read them; indicated 
by the lack of a common sentiment held by the participants and certainly not one that most 
people understood. According to the Manual, the goal of the event was to make an 
environment fit for people to create and test systems in a vanilla setting while offering a 
competitive aspect (“Full Manual”). The lack of a clear goal in the eyes of the participants is 
indicative of the inadequate communication by event organizers, which then leads to a 
disconnect between the participants and organizers, hurting the overall event experience. 
Along with this, there were scenarios during the event where the lack of 
communication from event organizers actively hurt my own team’s “systems.” This mostly 
revolved around the mechanics of the event, mods, rules, etc. One of my teammates' systems 
heavily relied on the number of Nether portals allowed per team. We received unclear 
communication on this issue so much so that it was contradictory at times. The changes to 
certain mechanics were often hidden behind a thread on the suggestion or question board. An 
example of this is how my team, Ordonia, wasn’t aware of the wiretaps mod, while team 
Alpha was. Moreover, there were mods that neither team was made aware of. Inadequate 
communication hurts the results of the experiment, both in that inconsistent knowledge leads 
to inconsistent participants, i.e. uncontrolled participants, and in that it makes it hard for 
people that are trying to learn from the event to understand the parameters and context of the

Harlow 3
Systems Experiment. 
The lack of communication, however, is a symptom of another problem. Since the 
inception of the event, it has undergone many changes. It’s not certain how many were due to 
participants' suggestions and how many were merely the result of an organizer’s change in 
mind, but both of these avenues played a role. These changes were a misstep in the running of 
the event—they were often impromptu and unplanned while also being counterproductive to 
the goals of the experiment. To be clear, this is not coming from the angle of, “all change is 
bad.” A lot of the changes made by Turtle were good, and as I’ve outlined in my essay, “The 
Reactionary Nature of Popular Answers to the Two Week Phase,” anyone who adopts such 
an approach is mistaken. However, in this essay, we will consider the changes from the 
perspective of experiment design as well as participant experience where we find that they 
are counterproductive in achieving the goals of the experiment. 
While ad hoc decision making may sound like not the worst thing, or perhaps, it may 
even sound positive—what’s wrong with adaptability after all? For an experiment, it can be 
extremely detrimental. Changes introduce new variables into the equation, variables that 
weren’t in existence before. These new variables render any data in between the changes to 
be in different contexts. Assumptions made with previous data must be reevaluated in a new 
context. This ad hoc decision making is further fueled by the “Suggestions” board on the 
Systems Experiment Discord server. Allowing players to have an input is usually a good 
thing. It allows players to build what they want to play and deepens a sense of community. 
However, in an experiment allowing participants to significantly affect the experiment 
creates some problems. For one, obvious reason: It affects the outcome of the study, 
precluding scientific testing of a hypothesis. Even if your participants are running their own 
“studies,” these changes affect everyone, not just the participants who want the change. Not 
to mention that players are participants in their own experiments, which is opening up a 
whole other can of worms we will get to later. For these reasons, on the spot decisions just 
don’t work if you want to yield reliable results. 
On the player side of things, changes can foil any plans participants try to make. 
Especially in an event like this where planning is the name of the game, unpredictable 
changes can introduce problems that simply cannot be prepared for. Bringing us back to the 
Nether portal example. The rule was debated frequently, not only by participants but by 
organizers as well. The decision was only finalized nearly a week into the event. This meant a 
week of uncertainty on whether my teammates' system would actually work. The uncertainty

Harlow 4
surely has knock-on effects (i.e., frustration and burnout), resulting in the loss of players the 
event desperately needs. These effects are antithetical to the goals of the event.
The frequent, ad hoc changes seen above suggest a lack of foresight and planning in 
the design of the Systems Experiment. It’s understandable to want to meet the needs of the 
players, however, it comes at the cost of procedural control, a price that cannot be afforded in 
a situation like this. In that way, the Systems Experiment is sacrificing its ability to offer 
reliable results, compromising by pandering to participants’ own sensibilities. Ironically, 
these ad hoc choices also made participant experience worse; creating an environment where 
it’s hard to plan or even enjoy the event at all. 
While the name of the event is the Systems Experiment, Turtle has stated that it is not 
an “experiment,” and it was named the way it was for “branding” purposes (turtle2770. 
2026A, 2026b). Even if we suppose that its goal is to allow people to experiment with new 
systems, it blunders. You’ll frequently come across decisions that seem counterintuitive to 
achieving Systems Experiment’s goals. In the “Design Mission” section of the manual, it 
states that one of the event’s goals is to create systems that could “realistically be used by 
players in almost any server” (“Full Manual,” 1). This suggests a desire to be able to 
generalize the results of experiments to areas outside of the “lab” (turtle2770. 2026c). While 
this goal is stated, it is not seriously taken into consideration. 
One of the most glaring of these problems is having the designers of the systems be 
participants in their own experiments. It should be pretty obvious why this is a bad idea. The 
designers of the systems design them the way they do because they think it may work, 
hoping for it to succeed. This is clearly a conflict of interest. Consciously or not, the system’s 
designers will affect the outcome of the system in ways that would not otherwise be seen. 
There are scenarios in research where you may want to have a researcher “participate” but 
only as a perceived peer by other participants which can be controlled (this kind of researcher 
is called a “confederate”). 
 Further problems are found within the very nature of the event itself. The event, 
being a competition, encourages using and sticking with systems that might otherwise be 
faulty in the name of winning a competition. It creates a scenario where the players have an 
investment in keeping systems alive beyond their efficacy and material benefits. While this 
may represent some servers, it certainly does not represent most. It also discourages 
potentially malicious or otherwise self-interested players from interacting with a system in a 
way that is unexpected (i.e., a loophole). Even if such players are annoying, they are

Harlow 5
extremely important to understanding a natural server’s environment. 
Not only does the Systems Experiment present a conflict of interest in how it is 
structured. This kind of attitude toward non-invested players is enshrined explicitly into the 
rules of the experiment. Later in the manual, it describes the rules of the event, one of them 
being that “a player is not allowed to try to purposefully evade the mechanics of a system,” 
(“Full Manual," 10). A page below this rule, on allowing people to go without designing a 
system, states, “while it sounds fine in theory, this will introduce a lot of members who want 
to focus specifically on SMP style play. They are likely to get annoyed with systems over 
time and bypass them,” (“Full Manual,” 10). These rules may be well-intentioned, however, 
like with the structure of the event, they introduce a biased sample and a skewed dataset 
towards systems-oriented players. These rules are diametrically opposed to the goal of 
creating systems that could “realistically be used,” (“Full Manual” 1). 
Another sampling bias we see is due to the large amount of IMS members who joined 
the event. IMS members are interested in server design, and as a result of participants 
primarily being interested in server design, they consciously decide not to engage with certain 
features they deemed incompatible with the goals of the server. One of my teammates 
proposed that we went without using one of the mods used by the server entirely. This does 
not reflect natural player behavior that is necessary in experimentation; the average player is 
far more interested in achieving their own goals than in adhering to an idealistic purism based 
on a niche online community. This problem could be waved off as a failure in advertising. 
However, it connects to the issue of not allowing non-systems-oriented players into the event 
as well. The barring of non-design interested players from participating, whether indirectly or 
not, is detrimental to the usefulness of the data and therefore detrimental to experimentation. 
Despite it being the foundational goal of the Systems Experiment, the event wasn’t 
able to offer a testing ground that yielded generalizable conclusions. Thus, the “experiment” 
has failed to progress the field of MST. This is demonstrated by the biased effects that come 
from designers participating in their own systems, the nature of competition, and the 
exclusionary rules and invitations into the event. It’s an example of a lack of scientific 
integrity which should be learned from for the future. 
In this critique, we’ve seen a contradiction between the goal of a fun gamified 
competition (i.e. a good event) and allowing participants to test their own systems in a 
controlled environment (i.e. a good experiment). This contradiction ends up hurting both 
goals in the end. The event struggled to communicate with participants effectively while

Harlow 6
trying to listen to as much as possible. Decisions were made in the moment, hurting the 
research value of the experiment, while claiming the goal of creating a space for 
experimentation. Furthermore, the design itself discouraged reliable and generalizable results 
that can be applied to many different servers. Don’t take this as a call to change the Systems 
Experiment. As I’ve explained above, that would likely hurt the experiment even more. Let 
the Systems Experiment, my and hopefully others’ critiques of it, be a learning experience 
for the IMS in its forthcoming scientific endeavors. Let it pave a new path forward for 
Minecraft Server Theory.

Summer event announced with ongoing votes deciding server 
components 
IMSC: S-MA-2 
Background 
As the Institute of Minecraft Studies expands, the organisation has begun work on planning 
its first in-game event. The first-of-its-kind event is set to be held during the summer months, 
when most members are expected to be able to attend. 
The experiment’s democratic, member-led planning stage was officially launched by Turtle 
on 15 April 2026, a senior member of the IMS and head of the Department of Synthesis. The 
upcoming event is also supported by KingGame2000, who has obtained access to a server for 
a short period. The senior figures also worked together to establish the aim of the summer 
event. 
It was announced that “…each player would choose and operate a specific system within a 
single Minecraft survival server,” indicating that players will be able to control aspects of a 
Minecraft society to mimic a real-life civilisation. These types of “civ events” have long been 
popular in the Minecraft YouTube space; however Turtle clarified that there would be 
“[interactions] with the systems that their team creates to test them and create real dynamics.” 
The novel project will aim to simulate the real world as closely as possible to provide insight 
into how Minecraft players behave in the sandbox game, whereas most civ events are 
optimised for YouTube viewership. This distorts the real experiences and conflicts players in-
game may have, as a system of conformity is created through the setting of the server. The 
organisation also further emphasises the real and human aspect of the event, allowing and 
encouraging players to act freely and with their own will. 
This unique set-up will also allow some empirical data to be taken, which may advance some 
existing theories or disprove others.

process planning the event, emphasising its player-centric nature. Turtle’s plan is to continue 
to post daily votes until all server aspects have been decided by the membership.

New member-created logo for the IMS announced 
IMSC: S-MA-3 
After the name change of the IMS (from MSTI) on 17 March, co-ordinated and initiated by 
Turtle, submissions for a new logo opened. Previously the organisation used a block render of 
a server created by u/pietromarcucci on r/Minecraft, which was directly nipped off that post. 
Nevertheless, the IMS now needed to create its own identity and establish its own self. As in 
any transition, after you change your name, you may also elect to change your appearance. 
Further clarification and guidance was released a few days after about the contents of a logo 
submission, emphasising its need to be “recognisable” and be able to “attach meaning”. 
And so submissions began flowing in, and on 19 April, ten logos were able to be voted on. 
Design 1.8 by scorevon won in the end with 18 votes of 99 ballots. This result is obviously 
far from democratic and proportional, but ultimately the logo received positive praise and 
recognition. After some refining and creating the design in Minecraft, the IMS logo was set: 
an inverted cube with a command book at the centre, with a gray/green colour palette. 
I had a few questions, so I contacted the artist, who very kindly gave me a few minutes of his 
time. Most logos and brand designs are expected to be appealing and stick to your memory, 
but IMS is not a “brand” per se. When asked why such a usually dull and unflashy colour 
scheme was chosen, scorevon explained that “…the grey scheme creates a more cohesive and 
refined appearance.” Any design must consider its context, and this logo took into account 
the IMS’ professional and theory-oriented purpose. The organisation does not chase 
popularity (although it is important to spread our ideas), but instead scientific rigor where 
possible, deep analysis, and establishment of theories. 
Further, like how banks are made of marble acnd granite to symbolise stability, the balanced, 
stoic, and firm atmosphere of a gray logo showed to outsiders the IMS’ dedication to help 
members, and others, to “…create these systems better for their worlds.” The green sector, 
for me, ties everything back to Minecraft. That the institution is not a “wishy-washy fun 
police” that attempts to academicise the sandbox game, but to seek to improve the playing 
experience that many servers (and singleplayer worlds!) lack. 
Any change can either be for the better or worse, and I believe this will be a new slate for the 
IMS. Being one of the more veteran and senior members of the IMS, I always had a wish for 
the organisation to be a popular alternative interpretation of what it means to have fun in 
Minecraft. We are (probably) the first people to establish such a community, and to have it 
grow to over 200 members is a sign of our popularity. 
With this new logo and colour theme, we can make promotional material ahead of the 
Systems Experiment in the Summer, and the new banners and logos have already been 
applied to the IMS website. 
Finally, I asked the last, but very important question: “What made you join the IMS?” 
The creator told me he wanted to “…learn from other members, contribute meaningfully to 
the community, and play an active role in developing defensive systems in Minecraft.”

And my face began to grin. The space I now have such a huge role in contributing to is meant 
exactly for this — co-operation, learning, and creating. For such a long time we have seen 
servers rise and fall, promising great community and absolute freedom, hoping that players 
will bind together eventually. You cannot have a server that automatically makes people 
interact, co-operate, and build infrastructure without engineering it to do so. Our institute is 
now the home of these discussions and debates, and for this, I am intensely proud. 
Moreover, the designer said they wanted “…[to have] political systems in Minecraft servers.” 
This is also another one of my personal goals in the IMS, where politics can be tested and 
tried with real players and people, all the while gathering data and creating theses to explain 
their behaviours. Having published the First Edition of the IMS Journal alongside my 
colleagues, we have already laid the groundwork for this kind of theory creation and a space 
where different ideas can be heard and given wide recognition. 
For now, the IMS will remain to be a small group of enthusiasts. However, with the Systems 
Event coming up, and some exciting promotional material I have been told is coming up, I 
have no doubt at all we will grow. We will become the home of debate and discussion on 
Minecraft Theory, just you wait.

A short rant about Minecraft YouTube 
IMSC: S-MA-4 
This will be an unusual article — there won’t be a lot of Minecraft specifically, but this 
articlle will be a broader discussion of discrimination in the offline world and what the IMS 
as an organisation can do to create a more inclusive space. 
CW: discussion of transphobia 
Background 
Two days ago, on the 29th of May, I published a video, originally titled “This Server is 
DOOMED to Fail.” What it’s about isn’t important, but what is is the fact that I reached my 
first ever 1k views after the first currency video. This meant that I reached more people than I 
usually do — including people who are not usual and familiar viewers on my channel. 
A few of these people then decided, instead of critiquing the video’s content, my analysis, the 
theory, talking about Raid Farms, or anything else, they would be transphobic. One 
commenter used the acronym 
“YWNBAW” 
a phrase originating from 4chan meaning “You Will Never Be A Woman”. Another said 
“[…]another one [sic] trans minecraft YouTuber?” 
Although not really transphobic, another viewer (if we can call them one) said: 
“mf sound like a real life pipsqueak” 
These comments are rare, but this reflects an alienating and hostile atmosphere within an 
already very male-dominated niche on YouTube. These people do not care about my content. 
They do not care about Minecraft at all. They have a particular hatred towards a group of 
people and they feel that they are permitted to project these beliefs on the comments section 
of a relatively small YouTuber. 
I won’t mislead you, transphobia isn’t a new invention in 2026. However, the current media 
and political climate, especially in the USA and the UK, are driving the endless ongoing 
onslaught of bombardment on this minority. They have a desire to drive trans, and other 
queer people, out of public life. 
So, if the bigots’ goal is to force me to detransition out of fear of danger, violence, 
harassment, or discrimination, what should I do? And specifically, what can we do, as queer 
people in the IMS and within Minecraft? 
What can the IMS do?

The mission statement written brilliantly by Turtle noted that the IMS doesn’t exist in 
isolation, and theories are not created independently of the world and society that we live in: 
“The Institute of Minecraft Studies works to explore and test systems in and through 
Minecraft” 
Moreover, the video game meant to unite people — friends and family — together must 
strive to keep this in its core. If we, as a queer people, want to stay in this game, in this space, 
in this community, we must, where we can, collectively do something. 
This brings us to the IMS — what can we practically do to make sure our organisation and 
our community isn’t transphobic, isn’t alienating, and is a shining beacon of inclusivity, away 
from the noise offline? 
1. Giving queer people a voice 
Not helping trans people voice train (although I know this may be popular), but allowing 
them to speak with equal opportunity, recognition, and scrutiny. This means we listen to 
them, whoever they are; allow them opportunities to express their thoughts on equal basis as 
cishet (cisgender and heterosexual) people, and not criticising them more than one would 
criticise a straight or cis person. 
This is why this Substack and the IMS Journal were created — to give ordinary members of 
the institute a voice to say what they want, even if they do not have the large platform 
YouTube gives. So, as I always have always said and continue to say, contact the board of 
editors if you want to write something! The Substack is always available even outside journal 
publishing cycles, but if you have a theory you want to publish for the journal, you may 
contact us on the same link too. 
2. Ensuring the IMS is an inclusive space, free of judgement or discrimination 
The most direct action that we can take here is through moderating the server effectively. We 
cannot allow any transphobia, homophobia, biphobia, or any other forms of hatred or 
discrimination on the server. We must be strict and consistent in fighting against anything 
that makes our server a worse place to be in. 
3. Action “through” Minecraft 
As Turtle wrote in the mission statement, the IMS works no online in Minecraft, but we also 
recognise the overlap between Minecraft topics (e.g. governments, economies) and real life. 
So, we must also do any and everything we can to include queer people in any servers that 
the IMS runs. This might be simply, again, moderating the in-game chat, but also doing 
active steps to ensure you have a visibly accepting server. 
For example, consider building a pride flag as the carpet for your town hall. Alternatively, 
think about how an event celebrating build by queer people could improve their visibility and 
dismantle and unfounded bias towards them. Host server sessions with quiz nights where 
some questions are about queer history to open players’ minds about this topic while also 
having fun.

I also have a gentle call to the straight and cis people reading: you have the power to dispel 
myths or misinformation. In fact, you have the greatest influence on those who are being 
hateful in telling them that their behaviour is wrong. Do not be the innocent bystanders who 
let someone being hateful slide. 
In a room of ten men, one makes a sexual joke about women. 
Two chuckle, thinking it’s harmless. 
Three silently fake a laugh, trying to fit in. 
Four do nothing, but watch them in disapproval. 
But none speak up.

Anarchy Without Ruin: Minecraft Bloodlines as a Case Study in 
Effective Server Design 
[By Miimuu] 
IMSC: S-MU-1 
Abstract 
Minecraft Bloodlines is, technically, an anarchy server. No land claims, no rules against griefing 
or killing, no spawn protection. But it does not feel like one. Where most anarchy servers 
descend into hostility and chaos, Bloodlines has produced a stable, warm, genuinely inhabited 
world through mechanics alone, without the safety-nets that most server designers consider non-
negotiable. The author has spent several months on the server and has found it fascinating to 
think about in terms of design ever since. Every so often, a discussion in the IMS arrives at a 
problem: player retention, community formation, or anarchy's inherent contradictions. Only 
Bloodlines solves this, and this paper attempts to explain how. 
Drawing on existing IMS works, this paper will argue that Bloodlines achieves, through carefully 
layered mechanics, what most servers fail to achieve through rules. Its birth system, skills 
system, semi-hardcore death mechanic, economy, moderation, and narrative atmosphere work 
together to produce a server that is communal, and that feels meaningful and immersive. It is not 
a perfect server, and this paper does not present it as one. It is, however, a masterclass in server 
design which the IMS can learn a great deal from. 
Introduction 
Minecraft Bloodlines (MCB) is a server that is difficult to describe to someone who has not played 
it. Long-time players tend to reach for metaphors: a living world, a family tree, a fantasy novel in 
which you are one of the characters. The feeling is hard to articulate precisely because it is the 
product of dozens of small design decisions working together, none of which would be so effective 
in isolation. New players, overwhelmed by the weight of mechanics and the warmth of strangers 
offering help, often describe the sensation of having stumbled into something they did not expect 
to find in a Minecraft server. 
This paper attempts to articulate it. MCB, created by Fantome, is best classified as a semi-hardcore 
anarchy server. It has no land claims, no rules against griefing or killing, and no spawn protection. 
However, it does have is a layered system of mechanics that shape player behaviour far more 
effectively than any ruleset could. 
Although the design of MCB appears to initially be problematic or flawed, almost every such 
theorised problem has already been anticipated and addressed by other mechanics. In order for the 
reader to adequately understand the complete workings of MCB and how it effectively creates an 
effective server, each mechanic must first be explained fully.

I. Server Mechanics 
The Birth System 
When a player first joins MCB, they are greeted by a black screen. The primary method of joining 
is to obtain two invite codes from two existing players, both of whom must belong to the same 
clan, and then use the /birth command in chat along with those codes. There are four clans on 
MCB: Aureval, Greyfen, Noctreth, and Virelion; and their function is largely cosmetic, determining 
a player's name colour. The restriction on code use across clans is seemingly intended to make 
pairing codes more difficult and to introduce a further barrier to entry. 
The new player spawns at the location of the player whose code they placed second, and receives 
the family name of the player whose code they placed first. Those two players become the new 
player's parents, and it is generally the case that the new arrival will be looked after by this family 
they are born into. MCB players receive one invite code every four days, and gain one heart for 
every two players they successfully invite. The alternative route to joining is through an original 
code, through which the new player is born with no parents but is then able to choose their own 
family name. These original codes can be obtained through channels such as Discord 
announcements, Reddit posts, or YouTube videos. 
Most players obtain codes by posting in the MCB Discord server, describing themselves and their 
playstyle, and being invited by existing players who judge them a good fit for their family or group. 
The birth system turns the act of joining into an economy of its own, and when there is more 
demand than supply, or more supply than demand, that shift plays out as a social dynamic among 
the playerbase. 
Hearts and the Death System 
MCB is a semi-hardcore server. New players begin with 30 hearts, and lose a fixed number 
depending on how they die. For example, 3 hearts for being killed by a player, 4 for fall damage, 
5 for a creeper explosion, and 50% of their maximum health for falling into the void. When a 
player's maximum health reaches zero, they die permanently and become a ghost. Their head drops 
as an item and can be picked up. 
After two weeks of inactivity, players die of old age (this is permanent). This can be deferred by 
spending Solins (the server currency) on a time extension, allowing up to five weeks of inactivity 
in total. Exceptions have been made where deaths by old age occurred due to genuinely 
unavoidable circumstances. 
Ghosts 
Permanently dead players become ghosts, locked in spectator mode and confined to a radius around 
wherever their head item is. Ghosts can possess a living player if that player stands still without 
taking damage for two minutes, at which point the ghost can control their movements until the 
player takes damage. Ghosts can speak in voice chat groups, and donator ghosts can also speak in 
local text chat. Ghosts can additionally possess and move armour stands.

The Skills System 
MCB features eight skills: Crafting, Farming, Fishing, Enchanting, Alchemy (potion brewing), 
Witchcraft, Clairsentience, and Cannibalism. Most skills impose significant debuffs at level 0 
relative to vanilla Minecraft, with the player moving progressively toward vanilla capability as 
they level up. Players are born with one innate skill (seemingly inherited from a parent, though it 
can mutate so a player is assigned a random skill) which starts at level 1 and levels up more easily. 
As what most of these skills correspond to is self-explanatory, the ones I have chosen to explain in 
more detail here are the most relevant (Crafting and Farming) along with those that are not self-
explanatory (Clairsentience, Witchcraft and Cannibalism). 
Crafting begins at level 0 with Makeshift items at 1/32 vanilla durability. Levelling up yields 
Assembled (1/20), Crafted (1/8), Handmade (1/4), Artisanal (1/2), and finally Immaculate items 
at full vanilla durability. Crafting experience is gained by crafting durability items, with gains 
generally proportional to material difficulty, and the skill uses a daily soft cap to prevent rapid 
progression. Reaching 99.9% progress triggers a diversity requirement, fulfilled by crafting 
overlooked items such as leather armour, shears, or wooden tools. 
Farming follows a similar structure. Crops on MCB take approximately a full real-world day to 
grow, though bees and flowers can accelerate this. At low levels, crops have a chance to fail to 
plant or to yield nothing on harvest, and animal breeding has a chance to fail too. These chances 
decrease with levelling. The farming skill also uses a daily soft cap and a diversity requirement, 
the latter fulfilled by activities such as harvesting nether wart or breeding rabbits. 
Clairsentience is a surveillance and investigation skill. A player places a clairsentience circle on 
the ground by crouching with an empty hand. Its diameter corresponds to their skill level. The 
circle records all interactions within range while it is placed: block breaking, chest opening, 
furnace use, etc; and when the player picks it up, they receive a message identifying who has been 
present. At lower levels, the player will only receive a message along the lines of “You sense a 
familiar aura,” and with some progression can only identify players of the same clan. At level 5, 
the full usernames of all detected players, regardless of clan, are revealed. 
Witchcraft is a ritual-based skill centred on arranging flowers and saplings in a 3x3 square with 
one in the middle and throwing ingredients into the resulting fire to cast spells. Spells have a chance 
to fail that decreases with skill level, and each successful ritual consumes four hunger bars. Spells 
vary considerably in effect: the circle of water with an earth catalyst will bonemeal crops in range, 
while the circle of earth with a water catalyst will cause server-wide rain. Circles of fire and air 
produce offensive effects, including shockwaves and persistent fire barriers. Witchcraft is not 
particularly central to the core gameplay loop, but its existence adds texture and discovery to the 
server. 
Cannibalism is levelled by eating Meat, a custom item dropped when a player dies that resembles 
raw beef. At level 5, players can consume raw meat, zombie flesh, and red mushroom stew without 
debuffs, which is a meaningful benefit given the food scarcity on the server. Hypothetically, this 
could create an incentive for players to kill in order to obtain meat, but in practice this does not 
happen and players usually obtain meat by collecting their own meat, buying other players’ meat 
or asking to keep the meat in exchange for collecting the items of a player who has just died.

Food Scarcity 
Food is deliberately scarce on MCB. Animals drop less meat than in vanilla regardless of farming 
level, making animal-based diets difficult to sustain. Suspicious stew and mushroom stew made 
from red mushrooms are poisonous, and on MCB, poison kills rather than leaving the player at 
half a heart. Farm-sourced food in bulk quantities, such as fish from guardian farms, carries 
debuffs. Mooshroom respawns on mushroom islands have been disabled, removing what was once 
the most lucrative food source. Practically speaking, the only reliable large-scale food sources are 
wheat farming and, for players willing to invest in it, the Cannibalism skill. 
Economy 
MCB's currency is the Solin, a physical in-game item that can only be transferred by hand. Players 
earn 15 Solins per day by logging on, with missed days accruing as a backlog. Solins are spent in 
the Catalog, the server's official in-game store. 
The most significant use of Solins is for purchasing hearts: one heart costs 1,000 Solins, which 
would require 67 days for a single player to save up for alone. This cost is steep by design, and it 
drives three observable behaviours among players: long-term personal saving, donating Solins to 
friends who are running low on hearts, and participation in informal redistribution schemes in 
which players donate their daily earnings into a pool that is then directed toward those who have 
the lowest max health. These schemes are made through formal agreements. 
The Catalog also sells immaculate gear, tools, and food, but at prices high enough that player-to-
player trade consistently undercuts it. This creates a natural economy in which level 5 crafters can 
earn Solins by selling immaculate items below Catalog price, generating demand for the crafting 
skill. Additional purchasable items include time extensions, group attestations (paper items 
granting access to the interface for groups), personal registries listing one's ancestors, custom clan 
banners, and the reputation book. 
The reputation book is available for 2 Solins and allows donating players to upvote or downvote 
other players and leave comments on their profiles. It is one of only three paywalled features on 
the server, alongside a custom soundpack and a custom arrow colour in chat. 
When a player dies of old age, their items drop on the floor, but only the Solins they had in their 
inventory (the backlog of hundreds of Solins for the two weeks where they did not log in is lost). 
The old age death mechanic in this way also prevents inactive players from returning after months 
away with enormous Solin stockpiles that would destabilise the economy. 
Cyclone Effect 
MCB has a cyclone effect by which mobs deal more damage the further from spawn a player 
travels. Zombies also give the withering effect. The overworld border expands with each new 
player and is currently at 120,750 blocks — its limit. 
Other Mechanics 
The day and night cycle on MCB is 24 hours, in real time, and locked to EST (UTC-4). Further, 
torches burn out after a while and so cannot be used as a permanent light source.

Wood cannot be obtained by hand (an axe is required) though new players can work around this 
by punching leaves for sticks, crafting wood planks with the sticks, and eventually crafting tools 
this way. 
Groups are a mechanic allowing players to display a group name above their head in-game and 
use team chat. Players can belong to multiple groups, and groups are used both for organisational 
purposes and purely cosmetically. 
Moderation 
Nytheon was originally the clan of all server staff. Players could receive Nytheon blessings and, 
upon death, would be transformed into Nytheons themselves, a process associated with staff 
recruitment, though some players have become Nytheons before joining the staff team. A newer 
clan, Elythar, now serves as the clan of server administrators, while the status of Nytheons has 
become less clearly defined, though they retain the ability to reap (ban) players. 
Both Nytheons and Elythars can appear in reaper form: Nytheons in black leather armour with a 
wither skull and black scythe, Elythars in iron gold-trimmed armour with a skeleton skull and 
white scythe. When a staff member kills a player for rule-breaking, the message sent in chat reads: 
“[Player] was slain by the Grim Reaper.” Even punishment is integrated into the server's narrative. 
MCB has no claims, no rules against griefing or killing, and no spawn protection. Cheating is 
defined as taking any action that gives a player an advantage over other players. In Fantome’s 
words: 
“Every mod is technically allowed on MCB. There are absolutely no ban on any mod. Only specific 
usages of game modifications are banned. In occurrence, any usage that confers an advantage over 
another player is forbidden! Quality of Life (QoL) usages are authorized! To determine whether 
your usage is giving you an advantage or not, you can ask yourself the question : "Is this specific 
usage of the mod possible to achieve for a player without it?" If the answer is "no", then you are 
gaining an advantage, and that's bad! :( If the answer is "yes", then you are not gaining an 
advantage, and it's just QoL! :D” (Fantome, 2026). 
Fenwych 
The Fenwych were a feature of MCB that is mourned by many players. A small number of players, 
upon permanently dying, ascended and became part of the Fenwych clan, player gods whose 
existence was never formally explained. Players could pray to a Fenwych by lighting a candle of 
their specific colour, and Fenwych could spend accumulated prayers to grant either server-wide or 
clan-specific blessings, such as faster happy ghast travel, haste, better enchantment success 
chances, or a brief window of immortality. Fenwych themselves could permanently die, although 
the way this could happen was tweaked quite often. To put it simply, it could happen if they ran 
out of prayers. 
On 21 April 2026, all Fenwych blessings were removed and replaced with a Final Choice: the 
ability to sacrifice themselves to restore a player's hearts to 30. The three remaining Fenwych did 
not choose this option. One died permanently. Eventually the other two accepted the choice, 
restored two players' hearts, and were brought back as Nytheons. There are now no Fenwych, 
though unconfirmed rumours of a future rework persist.

II. Player Entry and Community Formation 
One of the most fundamental challenges in server design is getting players through the door in a 
way that sets them up to remain. As matcha_tea has observed, a common failure is that new players 
join a server and immediately default to single-player behaviour such as mining, building and 
exploring alone, and never meaningfully encounter anyone else, eventually leaving because the 
server felt no different from an offline world (matcha_tea, 2026a). 
MCB's birth system addresses this from the very first second a player joins the server. Being born 
onto the location of another player, bearing their family name, and being expected to be looked 
after by a family makes social interaction structurally unavoidable. A new player on MCB cannot 
quietly log in and begin punching trees alone. They begin their life on the server in the company 
of others (unless of course they joined through an original code, but that is a very small minority 
of players, and the community that has been formed in MCB tends to help new players regardless). 
The birth system also controls population growth, a concern that the IMS has examined at length. 
Unrestricted player growth, as argued by Rev, leads to systemic degradation: interaction density 
decreases, spatial coherence breaks down, and administrative load increases unsustainably (Rev, 
2026b). MCB's four-day cooldown on invite codes means that the rate of new arrivals is tied 
directly to the size and activity of the existing playerbase. When there is more supply than demand, 
the choice of who to invite shifts into the hands of players. This captures an important quality of 
this system. Inviting a new player is a meaningful decision, not an automatic one. 
MrMillerPink has argued in the context of anarchy server design that birth-system mechanics risk 
creating large, insular gangs that push new players out, comparing them to predator-prey dynamics 
in which the supply of new players (the prey) is exhausted by the dominant group (MrMillerPink, 
2026d). This critique has real merit when applied to designs that use the birth system purely as a 
gatekeeping tool. MCB's design escapes it since the birth system here is not about power 
accumulation but about family formation. Players who arrive through the Discord server and 
introduce themselves genuinely are invited because they seem like a good fit, not because they 
represent additional manpower. Griefers and players who set out to cause harm do occasionally 
receive invites, but they do not tend to survive long, as the wider playerbase has both the motivation 
and the means to remove them. 
The birth system also solves, incidentally, the problem Rev has raised about pre-existing friend 
groups retreating into insularity (Rev, 2026f). Since each code must come from a different existing 
player of the same clan, and since players often post in the Discord server to find codes from 
strangers, it is difficult for a group of real-world friends to all join together and immediately 
sequester themselves. They are dispersed across the family structure by design, and the bonds they 
form with in-game family members tend to pull them outward into the broader community. 
III. Anarchy, Consequence, and Community Self-Regulation 
Perhaps the most striking evidence that MCB has solved what so many anarchy servers have not 
is a place called Kuawtitlan. On many anarchy servers like 2b2t and RaidFarms, the area around 
spawn is a scorched and cratered ruin, accumulated destruction rendered permanent by the absence 
of any social force capable of stopping it. On MCB, spawn is a city. It has a tavern, a temple, an

information centre, and the feeling of being somewhere that people have chosen to care for. It feels 
welcoming and is the kind of place a new player can arrive in and feel that someone thought about 
them before they got there. Kuawtitlan has sometimes been griefed; however the difference is that 
when it is, the community rebuilds it. This is not a policy or a rule, it is simply what happens, 
because the city belongs to everyone, and everyone knows it. The act of griefing it carries a social 
weight that no ruleset could manufacture. It is not forbidden, but it is frowned upon. 
On a server where a single player kill costs the victim three hearts and where permanent death is 
always a possibility, violence is not a minor inconvenience but a serious harm. The playerbase 
responds accordingly. Players who join with the intention of causing chaos tend to have a short but 
memorable career: they find their notoriety, enjoy it briefly, and then are hunted down and 
permanently killed by a community that has both the motivation and the means to remove them. 
The semi-hardcore death system is the driver behind the community's moral judgement. The claim 
here is not that violence never occurs on MCB, of course it does; the odd terrorist joins the server, 
and interpersonal conflicts happen. But players who choose to behave amicably and peacefully 
will very rarely have to face any violence. 
This does mean that MCB is unlikely to appeal to players whose primary interest is perpetrating 
violence and causing destruction, though even they are not entirely without a home here. The server 
villain, the player who rides their infamy for a week before being brought down, is a figure MCB 
accommodates if not exactly welcomes. Their story becomes part of the server's history, and their 
downfall becomes someone else's moment of heroism. Which is perhaps the most 
underappreciated thing about MCB's approach to PVP. Players who come to the server with combat 
as their primary interest do not find themselves without purpose. They can, if they choose, find 
themselves playing the role of protectors. When a chaos agent arrives, it is the PVP-focused players 
who organise the response, coordinate the hunt, and ultimately restore peace. 
MCB is, technically, an anarchy server. It has no claims, no formal rules against killing or griefing, 
and no spawn protection. What it is not is what most anarchy servers become. matcha_tea has 
documented in detail how the anarchic environment of RaidFarms collapsed into a hostile 
wasteland, concluding that anarchy is fundamentally incompatible with the goal of encouraging 
player interaction (matcha_tea, 2026c). MrMillerPink has similarly argued that even peaceful 
players on anarchy servers are driven to hostility by the presence of those who act destructively, 
creating a feedback loop that gradually expels anyone with amicable intentions (MrMillerPink, 
2026a). And yet, MCB, a server that began around the same time as RaidFarms in November 2025, 
is still thriving with an active and welcoming community. MCB does not avoid these dynamics 
through rules, but instead it avoids them through consequences. The semi-hardcore death system 
means that griefing and killing carry real risk for the aggressor. If the server community judges the 
act unacceptable, they face being hunted down and permanently killed. The Clairsentience skill 
means that griefers can be identified. The reputation book means that their actions follow them 
socially. The result, as Dragolantis's Community Rule Theory anticipates, is a community that 
holds the final verdict on what is acceptable (Dragolantis, 2026). 
Rev's analysis of moral transfer in Minecraft is particularly useful here (Rev, 2026d). Players 
import real-world moral sensibilities into the game, feeling genuine grievance at property 
destruction, unprovoked killing, and the deaths of tamed animals. On a server like 2b2t, this 
grievance has nowhere to go, as griefers cannot be found, named, or punished. On MCB, the

Clairsentience mechanic provides exactly the forensic capability needed to direct that grievance 
specifically rather than diffusely. 
Rev has examined the question of violence in servers, concluding that neither banning it entirely 
nor allowing it freely produces a satisfying result (Rev, 2026g). MCB offers a third model: violence 
is permitted but socially costly. Players who want to PvP in a positive sense become defenders, the 
community's enforcers against those who genuinely cause harm. Those who want to cause harm 
are free to do so, but will find it short-lived. The playerbase itself is the moderation layer. Rev's 
analysis of Engagement Theory helps explain why this model holds (Rev, 2026a). RaidFarms' 
failure was a consequence of combining forced proximity with no mechanism for converting that 
proximity into productive interaction. MCB creates conditions in which proximity is attractive: 
players are pulled toward spawn by the cyclone effect and the world border; they gather around 
the player-created spawn city because it is genuinely the most useful meeting point for trade and 
coordination. The community there emerges out of necessity, rather than being manufactured. 
IV. Progression, Recognition, and the Skills System 
Progression systems are quite well studied within the IMS, and for good reason. MrMillerPink has 
argued that wins feel empty without impact or reward, and that meaningful progression requires 
player agency, clear communication of information, and a sense of fair compensation for effort 
invested (MrMillerPink, 2026b). MCB's skills system satisfies all three criteria, while adding a 
dimension that purely single-player progression systems cannot offer: visibility to others. In vanilla 
Minecraft, there is no meaningful difference between a player who has been playing for three 
weeks and one who has been playing for three months, except in the resources they have collected. 
MCB's skills system creates a permanent, visible record of a player's history on the server. The 
player who has reached level 5 in Crafting and can produce Immaculate gear is recognisably 
different from one who has been playing for a week. Rev has observed that social recognition, the 
awareness by others of one's actions and achievements, is what transforms the individual 
experience of accomplishment into a basis for community (Rev, 2026c). The skills system makes 
that social recognition possible in a way that vanilla progression does not. 
Snorka's Five Motivations: accomplishment, discovery, connection, recognition, and domination 
(Snorka, 2026b), map neatly onto the skills system. Accomplishment is addressed directly: 
levelling a skill provides clear milestones. Discovery is served by the relative opacity of the skills 
system. Nothing about the progression of skills is explained to players by server staff. All 
information has been discovered by players themselves. Learning how to level up skills in the best 
way, and having only other players to seek guidance from, is itself part of the experience. 
Connection is structurally enforced: a new player with a low crafting skill level needs someone at 
a higher level to craft them usable gear, and the food scarcity mechanic means that farming skills 
must be cultivated collectively to ensure a group has reliable food. Recognition is built into this 
design. The Solin economy rewards those with a high level of useful skills with income, and the 
server’s community knows who can make what. Recognition is also relevant to the entire concept 
of a “bloodline.” If a player invites enough players and leaves enough of a legacy, their name will 
live on in the history of the server. Domination, for players who seek it, comes from reaching the 
rare heights of level 5 in a given skill and being known for it.

The daily soft cap on Crafting and Farming experience prevents the rapid accumulation of skill 
levels, ensuring that progression feels earned over time and that there is always a gap between new 
and established players that gives experienced players something to offer. The diversity 
requirements at 99.9% progress are a clever design touch as they prevent players from grinding a 
single efficient loop indefinitely and push them toward engaging with parts of the game they might 
otherwise ignore. 
KingGame2000 has identified focus, progression, and player agency as core pillars of successful 
server design (KingGame2000, 2026), and the skills system provides all three. The choice of which 
skills to prioritise and how to balance skill progression against survival is entirely in the hands of 
the player. The system provides structure without dictating a single optimal path. 
V. Economy 
Snorka has argued that a viable server currency requires portability, appropriate granularity, and 
utility (Snorka, 2026a). Solins satisfy all three. Being a custom plugin item, their value is set by 
their daily earn rate and by catalog prices, rather than being backed by a commodity, giving admins 
direct control over the economy's parameters using an external plugin. They stack to 64, solving 
the inventory management problem that plagues bulkier currencies. Their daily earn rate of 15 per 
player creates a slow, predictable accumulation without flooding the market. 
The heart purchase at 1,000 Solins is the critical feature of the Solin economy. MrMillerPink has 
identified the importance of economic sinks (mechanisms by which currency leaves circulation 
permanently) in any server where currency can be generated by players indefinitely 
(MrMillerPink, 2026c). Hearts function as the ideal sink: they are universally desired (all players, 
eventually, face death), expensive enough to require sustained effort to afford, and consumed 
permanently on purchase. The old age mechanic also acts as an economic sink by causing the 
Solins of inactive players to be lost rather than inherited. 
The secondary consequence of the expensive heart system is the emergence of  Solin funds, player 
organised redistribution schemes with no server-enforced structure behind them. The fact that 
players spontaneously created informal mutual aid systems in response to a scarcity mechanic is 
not a failure of game design but one of its greatest successes. It did not need to be designed,  as the 
server design created the conditions, and the community did the rest. 
The relationship between Catalog pricing and the player economy also rewards dedication. Catalog 
prices for gear are high enough to be uncompetitive with player-crafted alternatives, which means 
that players with level 5 Crafting have a genuine market. Snorka's concern that item shops could 
outcompete player trade and reduce the economy to a single shop experience (Snorka, 2026a) is 
pre-empted by the Catalog's deliberately extortionate pricing. The server shop exists to set a price 
ceiling and to provide a fallback, not to dominate the market. 
VI. Formal Moderation 
Where formal moderation does exist on MCB, it concerns cheating and severe harassment, not the 
usual plethora of player disputes. The theory which evaluates server moderation by Rev (Rev, 
2026h) provides a good framework to consider the effectiveness of MCB’s own moderation. In the 
paper, Rev lays out two key points: one, that server moderation consists of seven dimensions:

frequency, visibility, predictability, severity, proactivity, scope, and selectivity. Two, that different 
configurations of these dimensions produce recognisable structures of real-life institutions. 
However, in the case of MCB, its configuration is unique: 
On frequency and severity: punishments on MCB when they do occur are significant and entail 
permanent death or a drastic reduction in hearts, but they are reserved for clear rule violations. 
On visibility: the “[Player] was slain by the Grim Reaper” message makes enforcement publicly 
visible, which reinforces the legitimacy of the system without requiring constant staff presence. 
On predictability: Fantome's articulation of the advantage rule provides a stable framework that 
most players understand intuitively (Fantome, 2026). 
On proactivity: staff are known to actively investigate suspected cheaters rather than waiting for 
reports. 
On scope: staff do not intervene in player disputes that fall within the bounds of the server's 
anarchic ethos, which preserves the space for the community to self-regulate. 
The ambiguity in the advantage rule, with a lack of a concrete list of banned mods or clients, is a 
potential weakness, and is occasionally a source of uncertainty among players. In practice, 
however, the heuristic of “would a vanilla player be able to do this?” works well enough that first-
time violations of less obvious rules tend to result in warnings rather than harsh sanctions. 
Selectivity, in all known cases, is applied uniformly regardless of who the offending player is. 
VII. Narrative and Meaning 
This is a quality to MCB that is truly difficult to name. Players who have been on the server for 
any length of time will recognise it immediately and struggle to describe it to anyone who has 
not. It is not just immersion, though the server is deeply immersive. It is not just community, 
though the community is active and welcoming. It is closer to the feeling of being inside a story 
that is still being written, one in which you are not a reader but a character, and in which the 
things you do leave marks that outlast you. 
  
This is not accidental, but the product of design choices so numerous and so interwoven that they 
become invisible, which is perhaps the highest compliment that can be paid to any creative work. 
When everything contributes to an atmosphere, nothing stands out as a contrivance. 
  
Consider what greets a player who looks carefully at the world around them. Scattered across the 
server are in-world books by The Archivist: Notes on Clairsentience, Notes on the Cyclone Effect 
and others like them, written in a register that sits somewhere between field observation and 
divine instruction. They do not simply explain the mechanic. They treat it as a thing that exists in 
the world, with history and texture, and they offer their knowledge obliquely, in the manner of 
something discovered rather than taught. A new player who finds one of these books does not 
feel that they have read a tutorial, and these books do not offer any clear instructions. Instead, the 
player feels that they have found something. 
  
This is emblematic of how MCB handles almost everything. The Nytheon and Elythar clans are 
never fully explained. Their internal workings, their criteria for selection, the precise nature of

their powers, all of this is opaque, deliberately so. Players speculate. Stories circulate. When staff 
punish a rule-breaker, the death message reads: "[Player] was slain by the Grim Reaper." Even 
discipline is a narrative event. 
  
The Fenwych were the fullest expression of this sensibility, and their loss is still mourned. The 
idea that a player, upon permanently dying, might not simply end but ascend, might become 
something more — a deity of the server's own pantheon, capable of granting blessings to those 
who lit a candle. This gave MCB a horizon of meaning that most games spend enormous 
resources trying to manufacture and still fail to achieve. It cost nothing except imagination and 
the willingness to leave things unexplained. Players prayed to the Fenwych not because the 
mechanic rewarded them handsomely, but because the act of praying felt like it meant 
something. That is an extraordinarily difficult thing to make a player feel. 
  
The family system, the wiki, the historical preservation Discord server, the multiple community 
servers dedicated to different facets of server life, all of these are the infrastructure of a living 
memory. New players arrive already embedded in a lineage. They carry a family name. They can 
look up their ancestors. Older players speak about figures from the server's past with the 
reverence that one reserves for people who actually mattered, because on MCB, they did. Rev 
has written that narrative is what separates servers that die from servers that endure, and the 
distinction he is reaching for is exactly this: on MCB, things that happen are remembered, and 
because they are remembered, they matter, and because they matter, players feel as though they 
are part of something important. 
  
Just as Rev argues administrators should staff play the role of gardeners more than authors (Rev, 
2026e). The world is tended, not scripted. Server mechanics create the conditions for stories to 
emerge; the stories themselves are left to the players. What MCB produces, at its best, is the 
sensation of mattering, of existing inside a world that is paying attention to you, that will 
remember you, that will be different because you were in it. Players who have been on MCB for 
any significant time will tell you the same thing in different words: that they think about the 
server when they are not playing, that they have never felt the same sense of immersion in any 
other Minecraft server, that they feel something when a longtime player dies, that MCB has 
produced friendships and rivalries and stories they still tell months later. This is the consequence 
of a server designed, at every level, to make the experience of playing it feel like it means 
something. 
VIII. Limitations and the Conditions of Success 
Any honest account of MCB must acknowledge what the paper has so far only implied that the 
server's success is not purely a product of its mechanics. The mechanics are exceptional, but they 
operate within conditions that are not guaranteed, not permanent, and not entirely within 
administrator control. The most significant of these conditions is social goodwill. MCB's design 
is, at its core, a bet on human decency. The rebuilding of griefed builds is voluntary. The hunting 
of violent players depends on enough players caring enough to organise and act. The expectation 
that a new player will be looked after by their family is a social norm, not a rule. None of it is 
guaranteed by the design itself, and social goodwill is not a stable resource. It is produced by the 
community and consumed by it, and the conditions that generate it are not always within a 
server's control. This is important because community culture is vulnerable to composition shifts

in ways that individual mechanics are not. MCB's recruitment model gives existing players 
significant control over who joins, which has so far functioned as a reliable filter. But filters are 
not perfect. A sustained influx of players with different social expectations, whether through a 
popular video, or just the natural drift of a growing community, could begin to erode the norms 
the server depends on. The mechanics provide consequences for egregious behaviour, but they do 
not prevent subtler degradation in the form of the slow accumulation of players who are merely 
indifferent rather than actively harmful, who do not help new players, who do not bother to 
rebuild what has been griefed. The early game also deserves scrutiny. The server's design 
assumes a new player will be looked after. Abandonment is rare but does happen, and when it 
does there is no structural fallback. A player with Makeshift tools, no knowledge, and no family 
willing to help can have an experience that bears no resemblance to the warm, community-driven 
server this paper has described. The gap between MCB at its best and MCB when its social 
systems fail is significant, and this paper would be dishonest not to name it. 
 
However, the fact that MCB's success depends partly on its community is not a weakness unique 
to MCB. However, what distinguishes MCB is that its mechanics actively work to produce and 
sustain the community conditions it depends on. The birth system filters for players who have 
already demonstrated some degree of genuine interest. The family system creates bonds before 
any particular conflict arises. The heart economy gives players a material stake in each other's 
survival. The narrative atmosphere makes players feel that the server is worth protecting. These 
are not passive features. They are active interventions in the social environment, designed to 
make goodwill the path of least resistance. No server design can mandate that a community will 
be good, but good server design can make goodness easier, more rewarding, and more likely to 
persist under pressure. MCB does this better than most servers, and the fact that it still requires a 
community willing to rise to it is not a flaw in the design, it is simply the nature of the thing 
being designed. A Minecraft server is a place, and places are only as good as the people who 
choose to inhabit them, and who make them worth inhabiting. The fact that MCB has, for the 
time being, found those people is its greatest achievement. The lesson to take from this is that its 
design makes finding them and retaining them easier. 
Conclusion 
This paper began with an observation that MCB is difficult to describe, and it may close with the 
same admission. Writing about it risks reducing it to a list of clever mechanics, which it is, but this 
misses the point. The mechanics are clever because they work together, and they work together 
because they were designed with something specific in mind, which was not the maximisation of 
any individual metric, but the creation of a place where players want to be, and where who they 
are on the server truly matters. MCB succeeds where many servers fail because it treats player 
behaviour as something to be cultivated through design rather than commanded through rules. The 
birth system brings players into community without telling them to be communal. The skills 
system creates interdependence without mandating cooperation. The Solin economy creates 
exchange and solidarity through scarcity. The semi-hardcore death system creates consequence 
without barring players from participation. The narrative atmosphere makes players feel that what 
they do is part of something larger. 
The IMS has published substantial work on player motivation, economic design, narrative, 
moderation, and the specific failures of anarchy servers. Taken together, this body of work

describes a set of problems that MCB appears to have found successful solutions to, in many cases 
before that work was written. This paper has attempted to trace those connections, and the picture 
that emerges is of a server that arrived at success deliberately, through coherent server design 
applied consistently across every mechanic. The lesson MCB offers is a way of thinking in which 
every decision asks not just what problem it solves, but what behaviour it cultivates, what story it 
tells, and what kind of world it helps to build.
